title: SCOR's Third-Quarter Net Income Slips 4.8% to €206 Million as Hail and Storm Losses Lift the P&C Combined Ratio to 84.1%, With a New Strategic Plan Due on December 3
summary: SCOR reported third-quarter 2026 net income of €206 million, down 4.8%, with a P&C combined ratio of 84.1% against 80.9% on a 9.1% natural catastrophe ratio, a Group solvency ratio of 221% and an annualized return on equity of 20.4%, and said it will unveil a new strategic plan on December 3.
description:
SCOR, the French reinsurer, published its third-quarter 2026 results on October 30, and the headline is a profit that held up well despite a heavier quarter for natural catastrophes. Group net income was €206 million, down 4.8% from €217 million in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months, net income was €603 million, down 6.1%, and adjusted nine-month net income was €615 million. The annualized return on equity was 20.4% for the quarter and 18.9% for the nine months, or 19.3% on an adjusted basis. This article draws on SCOR's own press release as republished on a financial news site, and it covers only the figures in that release.

Property and casualty: a higher combined ratio

In P&C reinsurance, insurance revenue was €1,876 million, up 3.5%. The combined ratio, which measures claims and expenses against premiums, rose to 84.1% from 80.9% in the third quarter of 2025. SCOR attributes the increase to a natural catastrophe ratio of 9.1% for the quarter. Even so, the nine-month combined ratio improved to 81.3%, and the nine-month natural catastrophe ratio was 5.4%, within the company's 10% budget for natural catastrophes. In other words, the third quarter was heavier than the first half, but the year to date remains well inside the budget SCOR sets for these losses. The release does not name the events behind the quarter's losses, though other reinsurers have reported on late-summer hail in Europe.

New business in P&C was weaker. The contractual service margin, the stock of unearned profit on new contracts recognised under the IFRS 17 accounting standard, from new business was €142 million, down 16.1%. SCOR attributed this mainly to retrocession timing. Retrocession is the reinsurance that reinsurers buy for themselves, and the timing of those purchases affects how much margin is recognised in a given period, so the figure may reflect the calendar as much as demand.

Life and health

Life and Health insurance revenue was €1,881 million, down 1.0%. The insurance service result, which is the underwriting profit measure in the IFRS 17 income statement, rose 21.3% to €119 million, helped by a positive experience variance of €12 million. A positive experience variance means that actual claims were lower than assumed. New business contractual service margin in life and health was €93 million.

Investments

Total invested assets were €23.2 billion. The regular income yield was 4.1% and the return on invested assets was 3.7%. The reinvestment rate, the yield on money being put to work in new investments, was 5.0%. A reinvestment rate above the portfolio's running yield means that income should rise as older, lower-yielding bonds mature and are replaced, though the release does not make a forecast.

Capital

The estimated Group solvency ratio was 221% at September 30, 2026, up 6 points from year-end 2025. The ratio is the company's available capital relative to what regulators require, so 221% means about 2.2 times the requirement. Economic value, SCOR's internal measure of the value of the company, was €8.9 billion, up 4.0% as reported and up 11.9% at constant economics, meaning after adjusting for changes in interest rates and other economic assumptions. The release gives economic value per share as €50 in its summary and €49.77 in the appendix table, a small discrepancy between two parts of the same document that readers should note.

No guidance, but a plan coming

The release contains no explicit financial guidance. It says SCOR will unveil a new strategic plan on December 3. That means investors will not get fresh targets until then. In a statement, chief executive Thierry Léger said SCOR achieved another strong performance this quarter, across all three businesses, a reference to P&C, Life and Health, and investments.

How to read the quarter

Three points stand out. First, profits were slightly lower year on year but returns on equity remained high, which suggests the company is earning well on its capital. Second, the combined ratio's rise in the third quarter shows the effect of a heavy catastrophe period, although the nine-month figures and the budget comparison suggest the year is on track. Third, capital strengthened over the year, which gives the new plan room to focus on growth or returns.

The weaker new business margin in P&C and the lower life revenue are the figures that deserve scrutiny. The release does not provide the pricing trend in reinsurance or the amount of capacity SCOR deployed, so it is not possible to say whether the lower new business reflects deliberate restraint in a softer market or the retrocession timing alone. The company's own explanation points to timing.

Caveats

This article is based on a single company release and does not include the segment tables, the notes or the detailed reserve position. It is general information, not investment advice, and readers who need detail should consult SCOR's published results and regulatory filings.
image_alt: Storm clouds representing catastrophe losses for a reinsurer (illustrative)
key_points: Group net income was €206 million in the third quarter against €217 million a year earlier, and €603 million for nine months, down 6.1%; annualized return on equity was 20.4% for the quarter and 18.9% for nine months.
P&C insurance revenue rose 3.5% to €1,876 million, but the combined ratio rose to 84.1% from 80.9% because of a 9.1% natural catastrophe ratio; the nine-month combined ratio improved to 81.3%.

The nine-month natural catastrophe ratio was 5.4%, within a 10% budget, and P&C new business contractual service margin fell 16.1% to €142 million, which SCOR attributed mainly to retrocession timing.
Life and Health insurance revenue fell 1.0% to €1,881 million, but the insurance service result rose 21.3% to €119 million.

The estimated Group solvency ratio was 221% at September 30, up 6 points from year-end 2025, and economic value was €8.9 billion; the release contains no explicit financial guidance and says a new strategic plan will be unveiled on December 3.
why_it_matters: SCOR is one of the world's largest reinsurers, so its figures show how a company that takes on other insurers' catastrophe risk is faring in a soft pricing cycle and a heavy hail season. The absence of explicit guidance ahead of a new strategic plan makes the December 3 update the next thing to watch.

title: Hanover Insurance's Third-Quarter Operating EPS Hits a Record $5.15 as Catastrophe Losses of $109.7 Million Lift the Combined Ratio to 92.3%
summary: The Hanover Insurance Group reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $172.6 million and a record third-quarter operating EPS of $5.15 on a 92.3% combined ratio, with catastrophe losses of $109.7 million, net premiums written up 3% to $1.79 billion and $86 million of share buybacks in the quarter.
description:
The Hanover Insurance Group reported third-quarter 2026 results that combined a record per-share operating profit with a higher combined ratio, a pairing that needs some explanation. According to Reinsurance News, Hanover's net income was $172.6 million, down from $178.7 million in the third quarter of 2025. Operating income was $183.1 million, down 1.3% from $185.6 million. Operating earnings per share were $5.15, which chief executive John Roche described, in the words quoted by the publication, as record third-quarter operating earnings per share. Operating return on equity was 18.7%. The article does not report segment results or book value, so this summary is limited to the group figures.

How profit fell but EPS rose

Operating income fell by 1.3%, yet the company calls operating EPS a record. The difference lies in the share count. Per-share profit rises when profits hold roughly steady and the number of shares falls, and Hanover has been repurchasing stock. The release reports about $86 million of buybacks in the third quarter and $263 million year to date through October 26. The article does not give the share counts, so the size of the effect cannot be calculated from it. Readers should treat the claim of a record as a statement about EPS, not about total profit.

Premiums

Net premiums written, the premium retained after reinsurance, rose 3% to $1.79 billion. Net premiums earned, the portion recognised as revenue in the quarter, rose 3.9% to $1.61 billion. Growth of this size is modest compared with the double-digit growth that many insurers reported during the hard market, and it is consistent with a market in which rate increases have slowed. The article does not break out how much of the growth came from price and how much from volume.

The combined ratio

The combined ratio was 92.3%, up from 91.1%. The increase has a clear cause: catastrophe losses were $109.7 million, equal to 6.8 points of the combined ratio. The loss and loss adjustment expense ratio was 61.4%, up 1.6 points, which the article says was driven by higher catastrophe losses. Excluding catastrophes, the current accident year loss and LAE ratio was 55.7%, down 1.9 points. This is the more encouraging number for underlying performance, since it shows that the claims on business written in the current year, outside of the big weather events, were lower relative to premiums. The expense ratio improved to 30.9% from 31.3%.

Simple arithmetic on the reported figures shows how the pieces fit: a 6.8-point catastrophe load on top of a 55.7% ex-catastrophe ratio and some prior-year development gives a loss ratio near 61%, and adding a 30.9% expense ratio gets close to the 92.3% combined ratio. The release as summarised does not give prior-year development, so the reconciliation here is approximate and is not a company figure.

Investment income

Net investment income rose 12.7% to $131.9 million. Higher investment income is a feature of insurers that have been reinvesting at higher yields over the last few years. It cushions profit when underwriting results are less favourable, and for Hanover it was one of the main reasons operating income held close to last year's level despite the greater catastrophe load.

Capital return

Share buybacks of about $86 million in the quarter and $263 million for the year to October 26 show a continuing priority on returning capital. For comparison, the quarter's operating income was $183.1 million, so the buyback in the quarter equalled roughly 47% of operating income. That ratio is arithmetic on two reported figures and does not include dividends, which are not covered in the article.

What to watch

The summary does not say how Hanover is reading the pricing environment or what it expects for the fourth quarter. Investors will look for commentary on rate increases in commercial lines, trends in personal auto and home insurance, and the specialty business, none of which are covered in the article. They will also be watching whether catastrophe losses in the final quarter remain elevated.

For policyholders, the main message is that Hanover's underlying claims trends are not worsening, even though weather losses were higher. For agents, the continued growth in premiums suggests Hanover is still writing business, though at a modest rate.

Putting the quarter in context

Three features of the quarter are worth separating. The first is weather: $109.7 million of catastrophe losses is a large number, but it equals 6.8 points of the combined ratio, which shows how much of the quarter's underwriting result depends on events outside an insurer's control. The second is underlying performance: a 1.9-point improvement in the ex-catastrophe current accident year ratio suggests that pricing and underwriting actions are keeping pace with claims costs, at least on the business written in the current year. The third is capital management: with operating return on equity of 18.7%, Hanover is earning a high return on its equity, and the buyback programme is reducing the number of shares over which that profit is divided.

None of these points shows what happens next. A combined ratio in the low 90s leaves an underwriting profit of about 7.7 cents on each premium dollar before investment income, which is simple arithmetic from the reported 92.3%, and the quarter's investment income adds to that. But the figures say nothing about reserves for older accident years, which can move results in either direction, and the article does not discuss them.

Limits

This article summarises a trade-press report of a company release and does not include the complete release, the segment tables or book value. It is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: The Hanover Insurance Group (reported by Reinsurance News, October 2026)
image_alt: Financial charts and documents representing insurer earnings (illustrative)
key_points: Net income was $172.6 million against $178.7 million a year earlier, while operating income was $183.1 million, down 1.3%, and operating EPS of $5.15 was described by the CEO as a record for a third quarter; operating ROE was 18.7%.
The combined ratio was 92.3% against 91.1%, with catastrophe losses of $109.7 million adding 6.8 points.
The current accident year loss and LAE ratio excluding catastrophes improved 1.9 points to 55.7%, and the expense ratio fell to 30.9% from 31.3%.
Net premiums written rose 3% to $1.79 billion and net premiums earned rose 3.9% to $1.61 billion, while net investment income rose 12.7% to $131.9 million.
Hanover repurchased about $86 million of shares in the quarter and $263 million year to date through October 26.
why_it_matters: Hanover is a mid-sized US insurer with a mix of personal, commercial and specialty business, so its quarter shows what is happening when catastrophe losses rise while the underlying loss picture improves. Record EPS despite a higher combined ratio is a reminder that buybacks, investment income and share count matter as much as underwriting.

title: Hippo Raises Its 2026 Guidance After a 98.4% Combined Ratio and 60% Premium Growth, as Casualty Triples Its Share and Homeowners Falls to 23% of Written Premium
summary: Hippo Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 gross written premium of $498 million, up 60.1%, a combined ratio of 98.4% and adjusted net income of $20 million, and raised full-year guidance for premium, revenue, combined ratio and adjusted net income as casualty grew 146% to 38% of gross written premium.
description:
Hippo Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 29 that show a company changing shape. The headline figures are strong: gross written premium of $498 million, up 60.1% from $311 million a year earlier, revenue of $156 million, up 29.4%, and a combined ratio of 98.4%. The quarter also included a sharp drop in reported net income, which fell to $9 million from $98 million, but that comparison is distorted by a one-off item in the prior year. This article draws on the company's own release, of which only the first 100,000 characters could be reviewed, so some detail is not covered.

Reported and adjusted profit

Net income was $9 million, or $0.33 per diluted share, compared with $98 million in the third quarter of 2025. The company says the prior-year figure included a $91 million net gain on the sale of its home builder distribution network. Excluding that, the two quarters are far closer. Adjusted net income, a non-GAAP measure, was $20 million, or $0.74 per diluted share, up 9.3% from $18.3 million. For the first nine months, net income was $26.0 million against $51.7 million, while adjusted net income was $58.2 million against $0.2 million. Adjusted diluted earnings per share for nine months were $2.19 against $0.01. The adjusted figures are management's chosen measure, and investors should read the reconciliation in the full release.

Premium growth and retention

Gross written premium, the total premium on policies written before reinsurance, was $498 million, up 60.1%. For the nine months it was $1,312.7 million against $820.7 million. Net written premium, which is the portion the company keeps after ceding risk to reinsurers, was $149 million, up 26% from $117.9 million. The difference between 60% and 26% growth reflects a fall in net retention to 30% from 38%. In plain terms, Hippo is writing much more premium but keeping a smaller share of it, with the rest passed to reinsurers or other partners. Smaller retention reduces earnings volatility, though it also reduces the profit kept from each dollar written, and it depends on reinsurers continuing to accept the business.

A shifting business mix

The line-of-business figures show how far the mix has moved. Casualty gross written premium was $188 million, up 146%, and 38% of the total. Commercial multi-peril was $108 million, up 63%, and 22%. Homeowners, the line the company was founded on, was 23% of gross written premium. On a net basis the change is clear as well: homeowners was 50% of net written premium, down from 64% a year earlier. Hippo is therefore becoming less of a homeowners insurer and more of a diversified writer, and its growth is coming from casualty, a long-tail line where claims can take years to develop. That can make early results look better than final outcomes, a point investors in any fast-growing casualty book should bear in mind, though the release itself does not discuss it.

Underwriting ratios

The combined ratio was 98.4% against 99.6%, an improvement of about one point. The net loss ratio rose to 56.7% from 47.6%, and the catastrophe loss ratio was 6.5% against a slightly negative 0.3% a year earlier. The expense ratio fell sharply, to 41.7% from 52.0%. The improvement in the combined ratio therefore came entirely from lower expenses, since the loss ratio moved the other way. For nine months, the combined ratio was 97.9% against 118.3%.

Balance sheet and cash

Book value per share was $17.62 compared with $16.97 at year-end 2025, and tangible book value per share was $15.59 against $14.76. Total Hippo stockholders' equity was $469 million, up from $436 million. Annualized adjusted return on equity was 17.1% against 19.4%. Cash and cash equivalents were $311.8 million, up from $218.3 million, and total investments were $499.1 million. Nine-month operating cash flow was $124.2 million against $6.0 million a year earlier.

Guidance raised

The company updated its 2026 guidance. Gross written premium is now expected at $1.7 billion to $1.75 billion, up from $1.65 billion to $1.7 billion. Net written premium is unchanged at $565 million to $580 million. Revenue is expected at $585 million to $590 million, up from $580 million to $585 million. The combined ratio guidance improves to 97% to 98% from 99% to 101%, the catastrophe loss ratio assumption falls to 8% from 10%, and adjusted net income is expected at $77 million to $80 million, up from $62 million to $70 million. Stock-based compensation plus depreciation and amortisation is unchanged at $42 million.

Management commentary

Chief executive Rick McCathron said Hippo had a strong quarter, delivering a 98% combined ratio, and that even as the market softens it has been able to grow while improving profitability. That claim fits the numbers, but the expense ratio, not the loss ratio, drove the improvement, and the loss ratio is the figure most exposed to changes in claims trends.

Caveats

This article is based on one company release that was partly unread, and it presents management's metrics. It is not investment advice. Readers who need the reconciliation of adjusted measures should consult Hippo's filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
key_points: Gross written premium was $498 million, up 60.1% from $311 million, while net written premium rose 26% to $149 million as net retention fell to 30% from 38%.
The combined ratio was 98.4% against 99.6%, with a net loss ratio of 56.7%, a catastrophe loss ratio of 6.5% and an expense ratio that fell to 41.7% from 52.0%.
Net income was $9 million against $98 million a year earlier, which included a $91 million gain on the sale of the home builder distribution network; adjusted net income rose 9.3% to $20 million.

Casualty gross written premium rose 146% to $188 million, or 38% of the total, commercial multi-peril rose 63% to $108 million, and homeowners was 23% of gross written premium and 50% of net written premium, down from 64%.
Full-year guidance was raised: gross written premium to $1.7 billion to $1.75 billion, combined ratio to 97%–98% and adjusted net income to $77 million to $80 million.
why_it_matters: Hippo began as a home insurance start-up and is now mostly a platform for writing business on behalf of other risk-bearers. Its results show a company shifting from homeowners toward casualty and commercial lines and passing more risk to reinsurers, which changes both its growth and its risk profile.

title: AM Best Says Canada's P&C Industry Can Absorb Another 2024-Scale Catastrophe Year, but Flags Ontario and Alberta Auto Reform, Tariffs and Casualty Pricing as the 2027 Watch List
summary: AM Best analysts say Canada's property and casualty industry has the balance sheet strength to absorb catastrophe losses on the scale of 2024 or worse without threatening its stable outlook, while naming catastrophe frequency, Ontario and Alberta auto reforms, tariffs, casualty pricing and claims inflation as the issues to watch into 2027.
description:
Canada's property and casualty insurance industry is strong enough to take another year of catastrophe losses like 2024, or a worse one, without putting its stable rating outlook at risk, according to analysts at AM Best, the credit rating agency that specialises in insurers. The view was reported by Insurance Business Canada on October 29, 2026, based on comments from Alan Murray and Ravi Mittal of AM Best. It is a statement about the industry as a whole, not about any one company, and the article does not give the loss figures or capital ratios behind it. This summary therefore sticks to the reasoning the analysts described.

The headline view

Murray described the industry outlook as quite a robust one. In the rating agency's terms, an outlook is a view of the likely direction of ratings over the coming year, and a stable outlook means that AM Best does not expect widespread upgrades or downgrades. The analysts' point was that catastrophe losses have been running ahead of 2025 levels in 2026, yet the same framework still supports a stable outlook. They said that a repeat of the 2024 experience, or something worse, would be absorbed by the industry without threatening that outlook. The article does not state what the 2024 losses were, so readers who want numbers will need to consult industry data sources.

The framework, in plain language

AM Best assesses insurers using four building blocks: balance sheet strength, operating performance, business profile and enterprise risk management. Balance sheet strength is the capital an insurer holds against its risks. Operating performance is the ability to earn profit from underwriting and investments. Business profile covers the range and concentration of the business. Risk management covers how the company identifies and controls its exposures, including reinsurance purchasing. The analysts said that the same framework applies to the question of catastrophes, so the industry's resilience comes from capital and earnings, not from any special treatment.

What supports the outlook

Several supports were named. First, reinsurance conditions have been competitive since the 2023 renewals, a period in which primary insurers could buy protection more cheaply and on better terms than in the tightest years. The analysts cautioned that such conditions will not last forever, which means that the benefit could shrink if catastrophe losses push reinsurers to raise prices. Second, claims discipline has improved, and the analysts said that artificial intelligence is part of the reason, helping insurers manage claims more effectively. The article does not describe the specific tools or measure the savings. Third, higher rates have strengthened earnings. Fourth, investment income has been steady, which helps results when underwriting is weaker.

The 2027 watch list

The analysts also named risks to monitor into 2027. The first is catastrophe frequency and severity themselves, because a run of large events could test the industry even if it can absorb one bad year. The second is auto insurance reform in Ontario and Alberta, where changes to how claims are paid and priced could shift results. The third is tariffs, which can raise the cost of vehicle parts and building materials and so increase claim costs. Fourth, casualty lines such as directors and officers liability, errors and omissions, and employment practices liability are under pricing pressure, mainly in the United States, according to the analysts, and the concern is that softer pricing there could spill over into Canadian results. Fifth, defence costs for casualty claims in Quebec were flagged. Sixth, construction pressure in Toronto was named as a concern. Finally, claims inflation and climate risk continue to run in the background.

Earnings event or capital event

The key question for any bad year is whether it would be an earnings event or a capital event. An earnings event means that profits fall or turn into a loss, but the capital base remains sound and ratings are unchanged. A capital event means that losses are large enough to erode capital and force companies to raise funds, cut risk or accept lower ratings. The analysts' message, as reported, is that a repeat of 2024 would be an earnings event for the industry. The article does not give the capital ratios, such as the Minimum Capital Test used by Canadian regulators, that would let readers check this themselves.

What it means for buyers

For policyholders, a stable industry outlook is reassuring in that insurers should be able to pay claims. It does not mean that premiums will stop rising. The factors on the watch list, particularly climate-driven losses, reinsurance costs and claims inflation, are pressures on pricing, and the analysts' comment on reinsurance suggests that cheaper protection should not be assumed to last. Businesses buying casualty cover may see different pricing trends from property buyers, since the analysts describe pressure on rates in some casualty lines.

Limits of the report

This article relies on a trade-press report of an analyst interview, not on AM Best's full report, and it contains no figures for losses, capital or premiums. AM Best is a rating agency whose views are opinions, not guarantees, and the outlook concerns the industry in aggregate, so individual insurers may differ. It is general information and not financial advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Canada, reporting AM Best (October 29, 2026)
image_alt: Storm clouds over a city representing catastrophe risk for Canadian insurers (illustrative)
key_points: AM Best analysts Alan Murray and Ravi Mittal say Canada's P&C industry can absorb catastrophe losses on the scale of 2024, or worse, without threatening the stable outlook; Murray called the outlook quite a robust one.

Catastrophe losses in 2026 had been running ahead of 2025, but AM Best says the rating framework is unchanged: balance sheet strength, operating performance, business profile and enterprise risk management.

Supports named include competitive reinsurance conditions after the 2023 renewals, which will not last forever, stronger claims discipline, partly through AI, higher rates and steady investment income.

The 2027 watch list covers catastrophe frequency and severity, Ontario and Alberta auto reforms, tariffs, casualty lines such as D&O, E&O and EPL, Quebec casualty defence costs and construction pressure in Toronto.
The central question is whether a bad year would be an earnings event or a capital event; the article gives no 2024 loss figures, capital amounts or MCT ratios.
why_it_matters: Canadian insurers have faced flood, hail and wildfire losses in recent years, and homeowners and businesses want to know whether the industry can keep paying claims after another bad year. A rating agency's view on capacity, and on the specific risks it is watching, helps explain where premiums and availability could move next.

title: Aviva Canada's C$150 Million Settlement Ends Canada's Biggest COVID Business Interruption Class Action After Six Years, With Court Approval on October 16 and Fees of C$40.68 Million
summary: The Ontario Superior Court approved on October 16, 2026 a C$150 million settlement by Aviva Canada of the country's largest COVID-19 business interruption class action, covering about 49,000 policyholders in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, with no admission of liability and no ruling on whether the policy wordings covered pandemic shutdowns.
description:
A five-year legal fight over whether business interruption insurance should have paid for COVID-19 shutdowns has ended with a C$150 million settlement by Aviva Canada. The Ontario Superior Court approved the deal on October 16, 2026, according to a report published by Insurance Business Canada on October 26. The article calls it the biggest COVID business interruption class action in Canada. This summary draws only on that report and does not rely on the court order itself, which was not reviewed.

What the settlement is

The class is made up of about 49,000 policyholders in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia. Four Ontario businesses served as representative plaintiffs. The settlement involves no admission of liability by Aviva, and the court did not rule on whether the policy wordings covered losses from pandemic closures. That point matters because the central legal question, whether the policies responded to COVID shutdowns, remains undecided in this case. Settlement approval tests whether a deal is fair and reasonable to the class; it does not decide who was right.

Who is in the class

The class consists of policyholders who had restricted access endorsements or negative publicity endorsements. A negative publicity endorsement responds when an outbreak of an infectious disease occurs within 25 kilometres of the insured premises. Although the class is large, the number of policyholders who formally notified Aviva of a claim was much smaller: about 3,600 gave formal notice, and the report says 2,162 of them held the relevant coverage. This gap between the 49,000 class members and the few thousand with notified claims explains part of the settlement's logic, since the compensation process has to deal with a large group of people who may never have made a formal claim.

Timeline

The case was filed in July 2020, a few months after the pandemic began. It was certified as a class action in March 2023, which allowed it to proceed on behalf of all those policyholders. A six-week trial was scheduled for January 2026, and the parties settled through mediation before it took place. The article describes the process as roughly five years of litigation.

Why both sides settled

The report sets out risks on each side. Aviva argued that about 95% of policyholders had never filed formal claims, which would limit what they could recover. Class counsel pointed to the need to prove coverage, the task of valuing tens of thousands of claims and the prospect of years of appeals even after a trial win. Both sides therefore faced uncertainty about the outcome, and a settlement removed the risk of a loss for either side as well as the delay of an appeal.

The objections

Nine valid objections were filed with the court, and one objector attended the hearing: a lawyer acting for his daughter. The objection was that the claims protocol pays all class members for 30 days of loss, although her policy had a 60-day period. He described this as confiscation. She said her losses in the first 60 days were about C$500,000. The court held that representative plaintiffs owe a duty to the class as a whole, and noted that she had not opted out. The effect is that a class member with a policy that would have paid more cannot insist on a different outcome from the group settlement, unless she has left the class.

Fees and costs

Class counsel were awarded fees of C$36 million plus C$4.68 million in HST, a total of C$40.68 million. By simple arithmetic, that is about 27% of the C$150 million fund after tax, which is below the 27.5% allowed under the retainer agreement. The report says counsel worked more than 12,800 hours, with a billable value of about C$8.1 million, so the fee is roughly 3.9 times that value, a ratio the court accepted. The Class Proceedings Fund levy is about C$10.2 million. Each of the four representative plaintiffs receives C$15,000. BDO Canada is administering the claims process, which is under way.

What it means

For policyholders in the class, the settlement offers a structured process for payment but not a ruling in their favour. For insurers, the absence of a decision on the wording means that pandemic business interruption cases elsewhere may still turn on the exact policy language and on local law. For lawyers, the dispute over a 30-day versus 60-day payment shows how a single claims protocol can treat members with different policy terms the same way. The report does not tell us what the average payment will be, and with the fees, levy and expenses deducted from the fund, the net amount per policyholder will depend on how many valid claims are submitted.

Caveats

This article is based on a single trade-press report and not on court documents. It is general information, not legal advice, and class members should consult the official notice and the claims administrator for their rights and deadlines.
image_alt: Documents and a gavel representing a court-approved settlement (illustrative)
key_points: The Ontario Superior Court approved the C$150 million settlement on October 16, 2026, covering a class of about 49,000 policyholders in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia; there is no admission of liability and no court ruling on the policy wordings.
The class covers policyholders with restricted access or negative publicity endorsements; about 3,600 gave formal notice of claims and 2,162 held the relevant coverage.
The case was filed in July 2020, certified in March 2023, and settled through mediation before a six-week trial set for January 2026.

Class counsel fees are C$36 million plus C$4.68 million HST, or C$40.68 million, about 27% of the fund after tax and below the retainer's 27.5%; the Class Proceedings Fund levy is about C$10.2 million.

Nine valid objections were filed; one objector argued the claims protocol pays all members for 30 days although her policy had a 60-day period, but the court held that representative plaintiffs owe a duty to the class as a whole.
why_it_matters: Disputes over whether business interruption policies covered pandemic shutdowns were among the largest insurance fights of the COVID period. Without a ruling on the wording, the settlement leaves that legal question open for other cases, while giving thousands of policyholders a defined route to payment.

title: Star Health's Second-Quarter Normalised Profit Jumps 70% to ₹390 Crore as the Insurer Posts a ₹99 Crore Underwriting Profit and Its Claims Ratio Falls to 98.0%
summary: Star Health and Allied Insurance reported a 70% rise in second-quarter FY27 normalised profit after tax to ₹390 crore, an underwriting profit of ₹99 crore against a ₹40 crore loss a year earlier, gross written premium of ₹5,275 crore up 19%, and a combined ratio of 98.0%, according to a report citing its stock exchange filing.
description:
Star Health and Allied Insurance, the largest standalone health insurer in India, reported a sharp improvement in its second-quarter results for fiscal year 2027, which covers July to September 2026. The numbers below come from a report by InvestyWise on October 28, 2026, which cites the company's filing with the stock exchange. The primary filing was not reviewed for this article, so readers should check the original before relying on any single figure. The article does not include a loss ratio or a solvency ratio.

Profit: normalised versus reported

The company reports two profit measures. Normalised profit after tax was ₹390 crore in the second quarter, up 70% from ₹229 crore a year earlier. Reported profit after tax was ₹265 crore, compared with ₹80 crore. The gap between the two figures exists because the normalised number adjusts for the effect of changes in the market value of investments. The report says the normalisation assumes an annual yield of 8%. A normalised figure is management's choice of presentation and is not an accounting standard measure, so the reported figure is the one that matches the statutory accounts. Both measures moved strongly upward, which suggests that the improvement does not depend on the adjustment alone.

Underwriting turns profitable

The most important change is in underwriting. The insurer made an underwriting profit of ₹99 crore in the second quarter, against a loss of ₹40 crore in the same quarter last year. Underwriting profit is premium earned minus claims and operating costs, before investment income, so it indicates whether the core insurance business pays for itself. The combined ratio, which the report labels CISR, improved to 98.0% from 100.9%. A ratio under 100% means premiums exceeded claims and expenses. At 98.0%, the margin is thin, but it has moved from the wrong side of 100% to the right side.

Growth

Gross written premium rose 19% to ₹5,275 crore. Within that, fresh premium from retail health, meaning new policies sold to individuals and families, rose 35%. Fresh business growth faster than total growth indicates that sales of new policies are accelerating, although the report does not say how much of the growth is volume and how much is price.

First-half view

For the six months to September, normalised profit after tax was ₹775 crore, up 56% from ₹496 crore. Reported profit after tax was ₹815 crore, up 57% from ₹518 crore. Underwriting profit was ₹210 crore against a loss of ₹24 crore in the first half of the previous year. The report notes that this first-half underwriting profit already exceeds the ₹198 crore the company earned in all of fiscal 2026, which is a useful yardstick of how quickly margins have changed. Gross written premium for the half was ₹9,562 crore, up 19%, with fresh retail health premium up 36%. The first-half combined ratio was 97.9% against 100.3%.

Operating indicators

The report lists several operating measures. The insurer settled 22.5 lakh claims, which is 2.25 million, and its retail claims settlement ratio was 92.4%. Persistency was reported at 102%, up 4%, which is an unusual figure because persistency is normally a ratio at or below 100%; it may reflect a particular method of calculation and should be checked against the filing. The net promoter score was 65, up 4 points, and 97% of fresh policies were sourced digitally.

A conflicting headline

A separate search result carries a headline that Star Health's quarterly net profit fell 54% despite higher revenue. That headline does not match the figures here, and it may relate to a different period, so it has not been used. Readers comparing sources should look at the quarter and year referred to before drawing conclusions.

What to watch

Health insurers in India have been watched for claims inflation, hospital pricing and regulatory changes. The report contains no discussion of these factors, no loss ratio and no solvency data, so it does not explain why the combined ratio improved. Possible drivers, such as price increases, a change in product mix or lower claims, cannot be confirmed from the article. Investors will probably look for management commentary in the earnings call and in the full results.

For policyholders, the main point is that an insurer making an underwriting profit has more room to absorb claims, but profitability does not guarantee that premiums will not rise. For the industry, the improvement suggests that a large player can reach underwriting breakeven in health insurance, a line where several companies have struggled.

Reading the numbers together

Simple arithmetic on the reported figures helps put the quarter in proportion. Second-quarter gross written premium of ₹5,275 crore and first-half premium of ₹9,562 crore imply first-quarter premium of about ₹4,287 crore, so the second quarter was larger, which is consistent with the seasonal pattern of health insurance sales. Normalised profit of ₹390 crore in the quarter and ₹775 crore in the half implies about ₹385 crore in the first quarter, so the improvement in profit was steady across the two quarters. These are the reviewer's calculations from reported totals and are not company disclosures.

The gap between reported and normalised profit also deserves attention. In the second quarter reported profit of ₹265 crore was below the normalised ₹390 crore, while in the first half reported profit of ₹815 crore was above the normalised ₹775 crore. The two measures therefore moved in different directions between the quarter and the half, which shows how much investment valuation changes can affect reported numbers from one period to another.

Limits

This article summarises a secondary report of a company filing. It is not investment advice, and the figures should be checked against the filing on the BSE website.
